one_liner: NVIDIA's header-only CUDA C++ templates (CuTe) and Python DSLs for building GEMM/conv kernels; matches cuBLAS at best, wins on fusion and flexibility.
what_it_does: CUTLASS is a collection of CUDA C++ template components for writing GEMM, grouped GEMM, implicit-GEMM convolution and related kernels, covering FP64 through FP8, block-scaled NVFP4/MXFP4/MXFP6/MXFP8, int4/int8 and binary types on Volta through Blackwell (Rubin in preview). You do not call a BLAS function: you instantiate a kernel type from template arguments (element types, layouts, tile shape, pipeline stages, architecture, epilogue) and launch it, or generate kernels in Python with the CuTe DSL added in CUTLASS 4. A command-line profiler (cutlass_profiler) enumerates, verifies against cuBLAS and times the instantiated kernels.
how_it_is_fast: It decomposes GEMM hierarchically (threadblock, warp and thread tiles) to match the GPU memory hierarchy, staging operands in shared memory and registers and feeding tensor cores through mma/wgmma instructions. The main loop is software-pipelined (double buffering, multistage async copies), and Hopper/Blackwell kernels use TMA with warp specialization: producer warps load, consumer warp groups compute, in persistent cooperative or ping-pong schedules. Threadblock rasterization (swizzling) improves L2 reuse, split-K, sliced-K and Stream-K spread the K loop when output tiles cannot fill all SMs, and fused epilogues avoid extra passes over the output. CuTe layouts describe the thread and data mappings.
when_to_use: A GEMM or convolution that needs a fused epilogue (bias, activation, scaling, quantize/dequantize, reductions) that a closed cublasGemmEx/cuBLASLt call cannot express, so you save a separate elementwise kernel and a round trip through memory.
New or unusual data types on Hopper/Blackwell: FP8, block-scaled NVFP4/MXFP formats, mixed-input (e.g. int4 weights with fp16 activations), or FP32 emulation with 3xTF32 on tensor cores.
Grouped GEMM (MoE-style batches of different shapes) or awkward shapes where tile quantization leaves SMs idle and Stream-K or split-K decomposition helps.
Writing your own attention, normalization or GEMM-like kernels on CuTe or the CuTe DSL; catalogued entries such as FlashAttention-4 and QuACK are built that way.
Shape-specific tuning: cutlass_profiler --enable-best-kernel-for-fixed-shape searches tile configurations for one (m, n, k) and verifies results against cuBLAS.
when_not_to_use: Plain GEMM in standard precisions: no opened source shows CUTLASS beating cuBLAS; issue #11 (GTX 1080) has CUTLASS sgemm at about 93% of cuBLAS, and issue #3390 (RTX 4070 SUPER, 2026) has the public SIMT SGEMM 1.15x slower than cuBLAS.

Projects that need fast builds or small binaries: kernels are instantiated per type, layout, tile and architecture, and building all profiler kernels means tens of thousands of kernels, long builds and possible linker failures.
Windows builds (the README says CUTLASS 3.x builds are known to be down on Windows for all CUDA toolkits), pre-Volta GPUs (minimum compute capability 7.0, CUDA 11.4) and non-NVIDIA hardware.
Teams without CUDA template expertise who only need a stable BLAS-style API: the 2.x and 3.x C++ APIs differ, and the CuTe DSL is still marked public beta in the 4.8.1 README.

integration.form: header-only (include/ directory); CMake only for tests, examples, profiler and the generated kernel library; Python DSL as a pip package (nvidia-cutlass-dsl)
integration.dependencies: CUDA Toolkit; cuBLAS and cuDNN optional (used only as profiler reference/verification providers)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 host compiler, CUDA 11.4 (12.8 recommended; Blackwell needs 12.8, B300/Thor/DGX Spark 13.0); GCC 7.5 or 9+ (GCC 8.5 has known regressions)
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs compute capability 7.0+ (Volta, Turing, Ampere, Ada, Hopper, Blackwell; Rubin SM107 in preview); tested on Ubuntu 18.04-22.04; Windows builds broken for 3.x per README

gotchas: Hopper and Blackwell tensor-core kernels need architecture-specific targets (sm_90a, sm_100a): a kernel using SM90a features built for plain sm_90 fails at runtime, and sm_100a kernels do not run on RTX 50-series (SM120) GPUs.
Kernel choice matters more than the library: in issue #1567 a wildcard filter picked a SIMT (non-tensor-core) hgemm kernel at about 36,000 GFLOP/s against about 50,000 for cublasHgemm on a T4.

cuBLAS itself dispatches CUTLASS-derived kernels (issue #3390's Nsight trace shows cuBLAS running cutlass_80_simt_sgemm_256x128_8x4_nn_align1), so a hand-instantiated CUTLASS kernel usually ties cuBLAS unless you add fusion or tune for the shape.
The 4.8 README lists CUDA toolkit codegen bugs: some packed mixed-input ops compile incorrectly on Rubin (sm107a/sm107f) and are flagged rather than rewritten.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick CUTLASS over single-purpose hand-tuned kernels such as blackwell-tensorcore-kernels, gpu-compute or CUDA-L2 when you need a maintained, general toolkit with fusion, many data types and architectures rather than a win on one GPU and shape; those siblings report beating cuBLAS on specific shapes, which CUTLASS as shipped does not claim.
verified_claims_summary: Only parity is shown. A 2018 user run (issue #11, GTX 1080, CUDA 9.2, no flags) measured CUTLASS sgemm_tt at 2840.5 GFLOPS against 3065.46 GFLOPS for the CUDA sample matrixMulCUBLAS at m=640, n=320, k=480 (about 93% of cuBLAS); a 2026 user run (issue #3390, RTX 4070 SUPER at a locked 2400 MHz, CUDA 12.8, cuBLAS 12.8.5.5, CUTLASS 4.5.1, GCC 13.3 -O3, median of CUDA events) measured the public SIMT SGEMM at 19.696 ms against 17.124 ms for cuBLAS at 8192x4096x6144, and the README charts show percent of theoretical peak, not a cuBLAS comparison.
status_note: Very active (CUTLASS 4.8.1, Oct 2026; last commit 2026-10-20; 10.7k stars), BSD-3-Clause and header-only, so easy to vendor, though API generations (2.x, 3.x, CuTe DSL) and per-architecture targets change often.
